title: Neuro-Fuzzy Residual Fusion for Hybrid Retrieval: A Comparative Study of Ranking Quality and Contribution Traces
content: Hybrid retrieval combines lexical and semantic scores, creating a need for inspectable fusion decisions. We evaluate a residual first-order Sugeno adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) using BM25, dense cosine similarity and query-term coverage weighted by inverse document frequency. Its 27 rules use ordered membership breakpoints and yield exact decompositions of document-pair margins. A controlled, exploratory evaluation compares adaptive and frozen memberships, 4-, 8- and 24-unit multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), and a generalized additive model on NFcorpus, SciFact and FiQA. Models share inputs, candidates, starting fusion and training pairs. MLP-24 requires 4.7 and 3.4 times as many native terms as ANFIS to cover 95% of absolute residual contribution mass on NFcorpus and FiQA. Frozen memberships produce still shorter traces, indicating that adaptation is not required for the observed compactness. MLP-4 achieves higher retrieval means, fewer parameters, lower native contribution counts and faster cached scoring on both datasets. On FiQA, its nDCG@10 advantage over ANFIS is 0.80 percentage points, compared with 0.75 for MLP-8; multiplicity-adjusted intervals exclude zero. Comparisons with the additive model remain inconclusive. On SciFact, ANFIS and all MLP variants retain the initial fusion. The study provides a controlled assessment of exact reconstruction and identifies how contribution compactness depends on the scoring representation. These findings support neuro-fuzzy fusion as a structured alternative for hybrid retrieval and provide an empirical basis for comparing rule-level traces with compact neural and additive scorers. Human comprehension and cross-domain robustness require further evaluation.
